source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

At the bustling terminal, I stepped into the labyrinthine queue, my knapsack already emptied onto the metal tray before me. The officers’ uniforms shifted and settled into place, their movements deliberate yet almost ceremonious in their routine. Each traveler’s bag was scanned, checked, and rechecked under the harsh blue light of the X-ray machine before finally making its way through the metal detector. My turn came swiftly, the officer approaching from behind the barrier, her badge badge gleaming against the cold fluorescent lights. 

The officer gently reached for the ID in my wallet, her fingers precise, her voice matter-of-fact: "Please step back and remove your shoes." I did as instructed, the officer’s eyes never wavering from her task, her every move a silent testament to the protocols she’d practiced countless times. She pulled my coat away from my body, running her hand over my chest, then my waist and legs. The process, though familiar, was never entirely comforting. 

As we walked toward the registration area, the signs and instructions hung prominently, their message clear and direct: "Proceed at your own pace" and "Security first." The area itself was sleek, the tables covered in paperwork, the clerks’ faces obscured by their avatars. It was a place where authority spoke in concise directives, devoid of warmth but efficient nonetheless. 

I handed over the forms, my handwriting steady despite the stress, then sat down at the desk, watching the officer file my information into a digital record. With a final nod of acknowledgment, she left me alone with the waiting travelers and the ever-present reminder of our need for safety.

Beside them, the register of control was visible—its rows of instructions and signages mirrored the impersonal courtesy of the authority overseeing the controlled environment. The traveller’s nervous pace quickened as he waited his turn, aware of the scrutiny that came with every move and gesture.
